en.title: Third-Party Screen Readers: Are They a Security Risk?
en.summary: Unlike iOS, Android allows third-party apps to request accessibility permission, which makes it possible to develop screen readers for Android rather than limiting blind users…
en.body:
Published 7 October 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Unlike iOS, Android allows third-party apps to request accessibility permission, which makes it possible to develop screen readers for Android rather than limiting blind users to the built-in screen reader, TalkBack.

The presence of third-party screen readers has helped compensate for the lack of features and responsiveness issues in TalkBack. However, for a screen reader to work, it needs to be granted accessibility permission, which comes with powerful privileges that can pose serious risks if they fall into the wrong hands. The risks that come with granting accessibility permission, as well as the gains it provides, and the balance between security and openness, have been hot topics throughout the years. With the growing popularity of third-party screen readers, including new ones being developed recently with the help of AI-assisted vibe coding, the security aspect is becoming increasingly important to discuss and understand so that users can make informed decisions.

Before going any further, I want to state from the outset that the goal of this article is neither to give clearance to any screen reader or service, nor to accuse another of wrongdoing.

Table of Contents

The following definition is taken directly from the Android Developers website :

“An accessibility service is an app that enhances the user interface to assist users with disabilities or who might temporarily be unable to fully interact with a device. These services run in the background and communicate with the system to inspect screen content and interact with apps on the user’s behalf. Examples include screen readers (like TalkBack), Switch Access tools, and voice control systems.”

An article titled Accessibility Service – An Android Blessing and a Security Challenge in the Same Package from Bitdefender states:

“Android’s accessibility service is a powerful tool that allows people with disabilities to use mobile devices more easily. It’s also a favorite among criminals seeking to take over a device because it holds so much power.”

When granting an app permission to act as an accessibility service, the user gives the app access to powerful capabilities, including:

Although accessibility permission is built for services like screen readers, which are the focus of this article, it is also used by other apps to enable features that would not otherwise be possible. It is a core element of the popular automation app Tasker, and some launchers include an optional accessibility service to gain additional privileges.

Criminals and other bad actors have also found a great opportunity in accessibility services, which they try to seize and exploit to the fullest.

Google did not stay on the sidelines for long, taking active steps to make exploiting accessibility permission harder.

Since 2021, apps that use the AccessibilityService API have been required to provide additional information about their use of the API through Google Play’s accessibility declaration process before approval. Starting with Android 13, apps that are not installed from Google Play cannot simply be granted access to restricted settings, including accessibility access, by enabling the service from Accessibility settings. Instead, the user must first allow restricted settings for the app from its App info page and confirm the choice. Apps installed through some third-party installers can still bypass this step at the time of writing.

Google even restricts the use of unverified accessibility services when Advanced Protection is enabled, a mode intended for users who may face a higher security risk or who place a particularly high priority on privacy and security.

As stated above, granting any app the accessibility permission comes with a lot of privileges. However, in order for a screen reader to work, it must be granted accessibility permission. Without granting it this access, the screen reader is essentially useless, as its core functionality relies on the accessibility service it has.

Despite improvements, TalkBack on Android lacks many features that other screen readers provide. Many users find that third-party screen readers are more responsive compared to TalkBack, which still lags when performing certain tasks, such as scrolling, or on specific devices, especially those with mid-range or low-end processors. In fact, better responsiveness is an advantage that most developers of other screen readers use to advertise their apps.

No matter how we phrase it, granting any app accessibility service privileges poses a potential risk, even if the app is blocked from accessing the internet. However, this doesn’t mean that the app is really a risk, or that it is built with the intention to cause harm or steal users’ data.

The Play Store is the official app distribution store on Android. Apps are required to meet certain criteria to be hosted in the store. Additionally, Google performs security scans and checks to make sure that apps installed through the Play Store are safe. However, Google has its own set of rules that must be obeyed by developers who want their apps to be in the Play Store. If an app breaks any of those rules, it can be rejected from the store or have its approval revoked. Play Store rules are created to protect users, but there are restrictions that some apps cannot meet due to the features of the apps or how they work. There are app developers who decide willingly against submitting their apps to the Play Store, yet their apps can be completely safe, and the source code may be provided for anyone who wants to review it.

On the other hand, not having an app in the Play Store reduces the app’s reach, especially since it is always recommended to install apps from the Play Store as the safer choice for most users. People may also link the absence of a Play Store version to foul play, assuming that something prevents the app from gaining Google’s trust and being listed on the Play Store. As users should be more vigilant with accessibility services, it is understandable when a person refuses to install a screen reader that is not in the Play Store. However, not having a Play Store version does not directly translate to being a suspicious or risky app. There are apps that have functionalities that violate certain store restrictions, or simply apps whose developers don’t like to put their screen reader in the store. They could even opt for an open-source approach that is free from any store limitations, with both the updates and source code directly in the hands of users.

On the contrary, if a screen reader is on the Play Store, that doesn’t mean that it is completely risk-free, even if the risk is minimized. Bad actors are still able to sneak under Google’s verification mechanisms and land on the Play Store, with some apps gaining a high number of installs before being discovered. Additionally, accessibility services that are trusted by the Play Store could be doing shady things indirectly that affect users’ privacy.

It’s worth mentioning here that even if an app is sideloaded, when Play Protect is turned on, which it is by default, Play Protect scans the app for malicious software. If it identifies an app as potentially harmful, it can warn the user, disable or remove the app, or in some cases prevent it from being installed.

In order for a screen reader to be effective, it should work reliably without crashes and should be free of restrictions. Some Android UIs trust TalkBack as the built-in screen reader, giving it certain privileges that are not given to third-party screen readers, even if they are granted accessibility permission. Apps might also provide accessibility UI changes or expose data to TalkBack only, not to third-party screen readers.

For this reason, some screen readers spoof TalkBack by running their service and showing it to the system and other apps as the TalkBack package. Such behavior is not necessarily wrongdoing, even though an app generally shouldn’t try to make other apps believe that it is a different app, if the purpose is simply to enhance usability rather than to gain access to data for suspicious reasons.

Another example is when an app is given the ability to turn on and off other accessibility services. While this is not a straightforward process because it requires issuing ADB commands, it is still doable with the right knowledge. An app with such capability poses a serious risk, and I cannot imagine that it would be considered compliant with Google’s rules. But if the app is built to assist users in toggling between their screen readers, we look at the matter differently.

An example is the Shortcut Menu app, which is available on GitHub as an open-source project, and which I highly doubt could be approved for the Play Store if its developer decided to add it there. The app is built to give users an accessible way to switch between screen readers or to turn on another screen reader if one stops working as intended.

With the widespread use of AI, some screen readers allow the use of online AI services to describe content or perform OCR. They could also allow the use of non-AI services, such as translation or OCR. It is important to differentiate between the screen reader and the services it connects to. Third-party services are governed by the rules of the operators of those services, not by the screen reader utilizing them. This doesn’t mean that the screen reader is completely immune from responsibility. The screen reader should disclose the services it is connecting to, should encrypt data to ensure its safe transfer, should refrain from having any agreements with external services that allow user data to be misused, and should be transparent about everything it does regarding the data it sends.

Google TalkBack uses Gemini, which is also developed by Google, to describe and answer questions about content, but Google reassures users that the data is encrypted and deleted after the descriptions are received. Despite its bad reputation when it comes to user data, Google can be trusted with a matter like this one.

Unfortunately, this level of trust cannot be given to third-party screen readers. Jieshuo Screen Reader, for example, uses an online AI model from vivo to provide descriptions and answer user prompts, but there is no disclosure in the app itself of the exact model used or how the data is communicated. There is also no guarantee that the app would disclose if the AI service being used is changed.

As I am not a user of any other screen reader on the market, I cannot speak about how other screen readers deal with this subject. In all cases, using online services to analyse content should always be optional. If it is not, the user should at least be aware of the functionality that uses the external service so they can decide whether they want to use the screen reader or not.

Here, the advanced extension system found in the Jieshuo Screen Reader comes to mind. It allows users to run Lua scripts, which could be used to communicate with Android APIs, upload and download data from the internet, add, edit, and delete files and folders, and more. Just because the Jieshuo Screen Reader enables the use of Lua extensions doesn’t mean that it is responsible for the damage inflicted by malicious extensions. Users should be vigilant enough to avoid running extensions without trusting their creators, especially since these extensions and tools could be encrypted, so their code cannot be reviewed by the user, even if they have the knowledge to do so, or at least by one of the popular AI services that can review Lua code.

Jieshuo Screen Reader might be the only popular screen reader that allows for advanced extensions on Android, but Windows screen readers have this capability as well. If I am a user of NVDA and I decide to run an untrusted add-on, putting myself at risk, I am responsible for the risks I am knowingly exposing myself to.

With that being said, it is not possible to avoid criticizing how the extension threat is handled by the Jieshuo developer. All users can upload extensions to the Jieshuo servers, where they are discoverable by all Jieshuo users who go to the Extensions, Tools, or Gesture Scheme additional resources. Those codes are not vetted or checked, although their presence on the Jieshuo service could suggest otherwise to an unsuspecting beginner or average user. This user might go ahead and download an extension or tool, trusting its legitimacy, only to fall victim to a malicious one. Jieshuo Screen Reader poses a risk to those users, even if indirectly, because there should be a review of uploaded extensions and tools, or at least a clear warning when downloading those codes that they are not monitored.

They say that humans are the weakest link in cybersecurity, as many attacks are successful because of human error or reckless actions. With screen readers, the role of human error comes into play when installing unverified APKs. If you see a message on Telegram or WhatsApp that a new screen reader has been developed along with its APK, you don’t have to rush to install it. This could be malware waiting to take control of your device and data.

If you find someone posting about a new version of a screen reader you use, you don’t have to install and share this new version with others if you cannot trust the person who posted the APK. Popular screen readers have official places where they can be obtained. There are also reputable websites or channels that share official new versions when they are released.

Jieshuo Screen Reader, for example, is one of the screen readers that is widely shared in groups and channels, with modified versions sometimes being treated as official versions by users who think they are using the legitimate software when they are actually using a modified app. The screen reader has a GitHub page from which its releases can be downloaded, and new versions can also be downloaded through Jieshuo itself. There is also a website, although it is less known due to the lack of communication between the developer and the international user base.

Screen readers that are found on the Play Store are not immune either, as updates released through the Play Store can take more time to be approved and reach devices, and developers sometimes release versions as direct APKs before pushing them to the Play Store. When those APKs are modified and shared as the official versions, users may download them and put themselves at serious potential risk, something that could have been avoided simply by trying to find the official website or the screen reader developer’s channel.

Whenever an app hides some features behind a paywall, crackers try to use their skills to create and distribute pirated copies that allow users to access the Pro features without paying for them.

Putting aside the illegality and unethical nature of using cracked software, using a modified version of an app comes with the risk of malware being injected into it. This risk significantly increases when the app in question is an accessibility service like a screen reader.

The prominent example of a paid screen reader that is widely cracked is the Jieshuo Screen Reader , especially given the not-so-convenient method of purchase it utilizes . Maybe I won’t be exaggerating if I say that modified copies of Jieshuo are more widespread than official copies, with users sometimes even unable to differentiate between legitimate and modified copies. With so many cracked copies available, many users are put at risk of having their data stolen, as well as other damage that could result from running malware included in an accessibility service.

However, the screen reader’s developer cannot be held responsible for what a crack includes. In fact, the original developers are also victims, losing money due to unauthorized access to paid features, as well as suffering reputational damage because of the presence of cracked copies that could cause the original software to be flagged because of them.

A screen reader can monitor your banking activity. It can go further by silently entering data and simulating clicks without you even knowing what is happening, especially since a screen reader can alter the speech you hear or even perform operations without providing any speech feedback at all.

Many banking apps treat third-party accessibility services as potential threats, with some of them blocking them indiscriminately and others only allowing services that come from the Play Store. Others might flag a specific screen reader and refuse to run even if the screen reader is only installed but not running. While the measures banks take to protect users from unauthorized access and transfers are understandable, deciding whether what a bank does is an indication of wrongdoing by a screen reader is a different matter. First, the user must know why the screen reader is denied access and whether this is a measure applied to all third-party screen readers, to those that don’t come from the Play Store, or to a specific screen reader. If users are able to get the necessary information from their banks, something I doubt many banks would provide, their assessment of the security of the screen readers they use would be more objective and not based on assumptions or fear.

In all cases, denying access to banking apps and their data undermines the use of a screen reader, even if the user trusts that screen reader completely. I personally don’t like very strict measures such as blocking access to an app just because another app is present on the phone, since making sure that no unverified accessibility service is running while the user is in the bank’s app should be enough, as the user is free to use a certain screen reader elsewhere.

Some users might be very cautious when it comes to running third-party screen readers, especially those that are not in the Play Store, yet they might have a more relaxed attitude toward other types of apps that deal with sensitive data. TTS engines are one important example. Some people don’t realize that TTS engines can be used as a weapon against them and their security. A TTS engine that suddenly appears in a group or channel is still capable of logging every single character sent to it from other apps, including the screen reader. This data can be uploaded to external services, where it is analysed in search of potentially valuable information. With AI tools that can analyse huge sets of data quickly, going through generated speech output is now an easy task.

If you use TalkBack but have a TTS engine that is constantly consuming an unjustified amount of data, you should be concerned about your security, as the feeling of safety you have may be false.

Another category of apps that is popular these days is online image description and text recognition apps. Those apps connect to an external service, typically an AI one, where the data is sent and analysed to provide the information requested by the user. The number of these apps is increasing quickly, assisted by vibe coding, which makes app development easier than ever. The same points raised about screen readers communicating with external services are valid here, but there is also the fact that some users don’t think about what they are sending to those services through apps that are not considered risky accessibility services.

The previous examples are for apps specifically designed for blind people, but other apps can be security threats without requiring accessibility service access. They pose a risk to both sighted and blind people. For this reason, it is always recommended to check the permissions an app asks for, as well as any suspicious behaviour or unjustified use of a permission, such as access to the microphone or camera, or unusually high data consumption.

Opinions about the use of third-party screen readers differ within the blind community, with people at opposite ends of the spectrum.

On one hand, you find the highly cautious user who thinks that every third-party screen reader is a serious security risk, or even a spy agent harvesting every interaction, and should be avoided at any cost, with some applying this judgment only to screen readers that aren’t on the Play Store. While being reluctant to install potentially risky software is not a problem in itself, the issue starts when those people begin to make unsubstantiated claims. It is fine not to use a piece of software or not to like it, and to give your opinion about the risks of running an unverified accessibility service, but it is not fine to state your own thoughts as facts. Evaluating a software’s security can require procedures that include testing the software in a safe, sandboxed environment to analyse its behaviour and identify anything alarming.

On the other hand, you have the careless user who thinks that everything is safe. This is the user who doesn’t think for a minute before testing a screen reader, no matter where it comes from. This type of user is the one who argues that they don’t have anything to hide and that more cautious people are complicating the uncomplicated. Those users not only risk their own security and privacy, but they also risk the security and privacy of others, as we don’t live in a vacuum. We interact with other people through phones and tablets that could be running infected screen readers, and we connect to networks that could be subject to attacks. Those people increase the risk of data theft, impersonation to facilitate scamming others, and other forms of damage.

As with many other topics, our own subjective judgments play a role in whether we consider a screen reader secure and safe or not. Some people assume that a screen reader developed by someone from a certain country is a dangerous security threat, while one created by someone who resides in a country they trust is considered very safe. While it is true that some countries have better regulations and respect user rights more than others, criminal activities can be carried out anywhere. In fact, sometimes the reputation of a country’s strict laws can be a good cover for a bad actor to gain people’s trust. On the contrary, respect for users’ security and privacy can be found in the work of developers who might live in areas where the laws violate security and privacy. As they say, the person who knows the risk best is the person who has faced the risk.

Our biases are our own affairs that can affect what we trust and what we don’t trust, and it is a wise decision for someone who has escaped a totalitarian country not to use apps that come from developers in the country they ran away from. But we must present our statements as our subjective opinions, not as objective facts, if we are not willing or able to carry out the necessary evaluation procedures to determine what can be considered safe and what cannot.

I don’t have an answer to this question, nor is my goal to provide one. This article is an attempt to correct some misconceptions and raise awareness about accessibility services and what they can do. When you enable the accessibility service of a screen reader, you trust that screen reader, but at the same time, you agree that you are putting yourself under a theoretical risk. Those who follow my articles know that my primary screen reader of choice is Jieshuo , the notorious third-party screen reader. But many would not know that I remained reluctant to install this screen reader for years. Even now, I don’t have the confidence to tell people that this screen reader is completely innocent and safe, despite my personal opinion of it and my use of it.

I still have a tendency not to install new screen readers as soon as they are released, and I generally avoid screen readers that are neither on the Play Store nor open source. When it comes to open-source and closed-source screen readers, I lean toward an open-source screen reader free of Play Store limitations over a closed-source one found in the Play Store, provided I can identify its developers. Although I haven’t tested recent screen readers, I follow a few of them closely, with the possibility of installing them on my devices in the future. This doesn’t imply that I find the screen reader I use more secure than the screen readers I haven’t installed. In fact, the opposite could be true. Yet, I still stick to what I use because I have adapted my usage to the screen reader that I have used for years, without ignoring the possibility that something could go wrong one day.

Screen reader developers should be transparent about what data they collect, which external services they communicate with, and how they communicate with those services. When they offer advanced capabilities such as extensions,they should alert users to the risks of using unverified extensions instead of giving them a false sense of safety by letting them explore unvetted extensions or making it very easy to run extensions without any proper warning.

Whatever comes with the accessibility permission, restricting it is not the solution, as these restrictions cause more harm than they prevent. The solution lies in the hands of users, who should use common sense when they want to install a third-party accessibility service. Look at the gains versus the potential risks. Stay away from APKs from unknown sources, and don’t come near cracks. Keep Play Protect scanning for sideloaded apps enabled. Distinguish between the real risks of a screen reader and human error or recklessness. Look for any red flags, but don’t try to dictate your preferences as established facts.

es.title: Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3
es.summary: Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación, la beta 4 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, … Continuar leyendo "Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3" La entrada Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .
es.body:
Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación , la beta 4 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, o por el sistema de informe de fallos de NV Access . Esta versión no es apta para entornos de producción. Al instalar esta beta te unirás al canal beta, y sólo recibirás avisos de actualización de compilaciones beta y candidatas a liberación (rc). El canal beta/rc siempre te mantendrá al día con la versión más reciente de NVDA. La última rc de un ciclo de liberación es idéntica a la última versión estable. Para regresar al canal de versiones estables, instala a mano la última versión estable.

Esta versión incorpora importantes mejoras de rendimiento, mejoras en los diálogos de NVDA, y entrada expandida por la pantalla táctil. Se han hecho varias mejoras para reducir los retrasos y aumentar el rendimiento. Ahora NVDA recupera y captura más información sobre los controles en segundo plano, mejorando el rendimiento en controles como cuadros combinados y el explorador de archivos. NVDA ya no hace que se rompan el explorador de archivos u otras aplicaciones al cerrarlo o reiniciarlo. NVDA se recupera ahora más rápido cuando una aplicación deja de responder, y ya no se colgará ni inundará el registro con errores en aplicaciones que no responden. En regiones vivas de texto, como las terminales, NVDA ya no se cuelga cuando se vuelcan en pantalla importantes cantidades de texto. Se han añadido menús de contexto y atajos de teclado a los diálogos de perfiles de configuración, gestos de entrada y diccionarios del habla, haciendo que estos diálogos sean más fáciles de usar con el teclado. Ahora también es posible cambiar directamente un gesto existente en el diálogo Gestos de entrada. Se ha modernizado el diálogo que presenta mensajes explorables y ahora soporta mejor cambiar su tamaño, maximizarlo y minimizarlo. Se ha expandido significativamente la entrada por pantalla táctil. Los gestos de dos deslizamientos secuenciales ahora combinan dos deslizamientos en rápida sucesión en un solo gesto, incrementando enormemente la cantidad de gestos asociables. También se soportan ahora los gestos de borde, permitiendo que los gestos que comiencen a 15 mm de cualquier borde de la pantalla se asocien independientemente de los mismos gestos realizados en el centro de la pantalla. Se ha añadido una nueva orden sin asignar para mover el cursor del ratón al centro de la vista ampliada. Se puede usar el OCR de Windows con la lupa o la cortina de pantalla activadas. Se ha actualizado Liblouis con nuevas tablas braille en Elfdaliano, sami, maorí, braille unificado inglés de Nueva Zelanda, y aitiano criollo, una tabla noruega para texto en español, y variantes adicionales de sueco de 6 y 8 puntos. Se ha actualizado Espeak NG añadiendo soporte para liguriano y abkhaz. Para instalar esta beta, puedes configurar el canal «rc y beta» en el complemento Selector del canal de actualización y buscar actualizaciones desde el menú Ayuda de NVDA, o actualizar desde una beta anterior. Y como siempre, también puedes descargar manualmente el instalador de NVDA 2026.3 beta 4 . Su suma de comprobación SHA256, que te permitirá garantizar la integridad del archivo descargado, es 8be91476179710c4abffe5094459df9be1696d92e5d6cd0ace47d52321bb87ab. ¡Feliz martes!

La entrada Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .

en.title: Shortcut Menu
en.summary: Shortcut Menu lets the Android accessibility shortcut, such as holding both volume keys, turn your choice of screen reader or other accessibility service on or…
en.body:
Published 3 October 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Shortcut Menu lets the Android accessibility shortcut, such as holding both volume keys, turn your choice of screen reader or other accessibility service on or off. It works like the accessibility shortcut menu on iPhone:

Turning a screen reader on turns any other screen reader off, so two never talk at once. Services with the same name, such as Google’s and Samsung’s TalkBack, are told apart by their maker, such as “TalkBack (Samsung)”. Pressing the shortcut again while the menu is open closes it.

Without Shortcut Menu, a shortcut with more than one feature on it asks which one to use, and that question is not spoken when no screen reader is on.

With Shizuku, run the same command without adb shell. In Settings, Accessibility, open Shortcut Menu and turn on its shortcut, such as the volume keys. Make Shortcut Menu the only feature on that shortcut. Open the Shortcut Menu app and choose which services the menu offers. Until you choose, it offers your screen readers. The app also shows whether the permission is granted and what each shortcut is assigned to, and has a button to try the menu. How it works The shortcut turns Shortcut Menu’s accessibility service on, and the service opens the menu. When the menu closes, the service turns itself off, so the next press turns it on again. A press while the menu is open turns the service off, which closes the menu.

Choosing a service changes Android’s list of enabled accessibility services directly, so Android does not ask “Allow full control?” each time. The menu speaks with the phone’s text-to-speech engine, at the accessibility volume.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Samsung UI is the only Android UI that offers 3 accessibility shortcuts: pressing and holding the volume keys, short pressing the power and volume up keys, and the accessibility onscreen button or gesture, based on the navigation mode being used. Other OEMs offer only the first and third shortcuts. Honor even excludes the accessibility button and gesture, leaving the user with only 1 shortcut, and that shortcut can only be assigned to 1 accessibility service. On UIs that allow more than 1 accessibility service to be assigned to the shortcut, Android asks the user to choose which one to activate every time the shortcut is used. However, this dialog is not accessible if no screen reader is running.

Shortcut Menu aims to address these shortcomings by allowing the user to choose the accessibility services they want to launch from the shortcut. The user can then launch any of the selected services in an accessible way. When no screen reader is active, the service speaks the items as the user moves their finger over them, and lifting the finger activates the selected service. If a screen reader is already active, the service makes sure to turn it off before launching another screen reader to avoid potential conflicts.

Setting up the app requires an ADB command, which can be run either using ADB on a computer or directly on the phone through an ADB app that uses wireless debugging. Working with ADB is not covered here, but I personally used the ADB AppControl mobile app to enter the command that grants the app the required permission.

The app's UI is straightforward. It shows whether the permission has been granted and which shortcut is assigned to the service. It also includes a menu where you can turn services on or off without using the shortcut. The user can select which services should be included, although screen readers are checked by default. For me, Jieshuo Main, Jieshuo Helper Service, TalkBack, and AI Subtitles were all included.

When using the shortcut, the app currently speaks through Google TTS. When a screen reader is active, it behaves like a regular screen that the screen reader can interact with.

For Samsung users who keep both Samsung TalkBack and Google's TalkBack on their devices and wish to switch between them, both can be added to the services list. I haven't tested this on a Samsung device to see if there are any issues. Anyway, starting with One UI 9, Samsung TalkBack is replaced with Google TalkBack, so there are no longer two TalkBack versions.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

App version: 0.2, Android 16

★★★★★ 5.0 / 5 based on 1 rating

Please use this rating only for accessibility. For feedback about the app’s features, price, overall quality, or your general experience, use the comments section below.

en.title: Lexo Offline AI Voice Keyboard
en.summary: Lexo is a private AI keyboard for Android. Voice typing and next-word prediction both run entirely on device, so once setup is done the keyboard…
en.body:
Published 1 October 2026 by Warren Carr

Lexo is a private AI keyboard for Android. Voice typing and next-word prediction both run entirely on device, so once setup is done the keyboard keeps working with no internet connection, in airplane mode, and anywhere the signal drops.

After installing, open Lexo once to switch it on. The app walks you through it: pick your language, turn Lexo on in Android’s keyboard settings, make it your keyboard, then try it out.

Cloud keyboards send what you type to a server and wait for the answer. Lexo puts the models on your phone instead: the typing model downloads once, plus the speech recognizer if you use voice, then they live in the app’s private storage. Nothing you type or say leaves the phone. No sign-up, no ads.

Lexo is a paid keyboard. Every install starts with a 30-day Premium trial covering everything the on-device models power: offline voice typing, next-word prediction, the suggestion strip and autocorrect, and glide typing.

After that those features stop until you buy Premium: a one-time purchase, not a subscription. Without Premium the keyboard still types: layouts, language switching, emoji, clipboard history, themes, one-handed mode and gestures. No ads either way.

Setup downloads the typing model for your language once, over Wi-Fi by default. Its size depends on the language. Voice typing downloads its own speech pack the first time you use the microphone, and each extra language adds its own. App updates do not re-download any of it.

Built on the open-source FlorisBoard project, with open-weight models: SmolLM2, Qwen2.5 and KB-Whisper (Apache-2.0), a Turkish GPT-2 fine-tune (MIT), Gemma (Gemma Terms of Use) and NVIDIA Parakeet (CC-BY-4.0).

Questions, bug reports, feature requests: reddit.com/r/lexokeyboard .

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Following the release of the Pixel 11-series that came onboard with “Rambler,” a new experience of voice typing, more and more Devs are coming up with creative methods of achieving the same experience for non-Pixel 11-series users. Thus, we’re here talking about “Lexo Keyboard,” a keyboard that works entirely offline once you download the model needed for offline use.

I spent a lot of time working with the Developer to make the app accessible, and I’m proud of this Developer for his work in ensuring that the keyboard is accessible.

Thus, the keyboard supports “lift-to-type” using TalkBack.

I put the keyboard to use on both my Galaxy S23+, running One UI 8.5 (Android 16), and my Pixel 11 Pro XL, running Android 17. The voice dictation works similarly across the two devices.

What is worth mentioning, however, is that in order to be able to double-tap anywhere on the phone to stop voice dictation, you would have to go to TalkBack Settings > Advanced settings > Reduce delay > Typing preference and choose “Hold finger to select letter key, then lift. Double-tap for other keys.”

If you use “Hold finger to select any key, then lift” instead, you need to tap the voice input key directly to stop voice input, as tapping outside the keyboard area won’t stop it.

There are lots of settings on the keyboard that you can customize to your liking. Take advantage of those and customize the keyboard to your liking.

The app is available to anyone with access to the Play Store. When it comes to pricing, there’s a one-time payment of 10 bucks. Without the one-time payment, you can use the app with all features enabled for a period of 30 days.

After those 30 days, you wouldn’t have access to the premium features, but even as a free user outside of the 30-day free period, there are no ads.

You can listen to my Blind Android Users podcast audio demo of the keyboard Here

Last Tested App version and Android version:

2.0.37. Android 17

No accessibility ratings yet. Be the first to rate this app.

en.title: What’s New In Jieshuo 20261001
en.summary: Version 20261001 of the Jieshuo screen reader has been released. Here are the main additions and changes in this version. Support For External AI Models…
en.body:
Published 1 October 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Version 20261001 of the Jieshuo screen reader has been released. Here are the main additions and changes in this version.

Table of Contents

Jieshuo now supports using external AI models for a number of its AI-powered functions.

The new release allows users to set their preferred AI services for the following functions:

I assume that the functions related to the focused item also cover the corresponding functions that work on the entire screen, such as inquire by voice and detailed description. However, I cannot say this for sure because I have not tested these functions myself.

To set the models, go to Screen reader settings > Advanced settings > the section that is still in Chinese. There is a toggle for each function to enable the use of a custom AI model, and you can configure a different model for each function. You can customize the necessary parameters, such as the URL of an OpenAI-compatible AI service, model name, prompt, and API key. There is also a Test button that you can use to check whether the configuration works.

This feature is available to paid users only.

Jieshuo now includes new presets for the speech output audio. These are available in a new section that is still in Chinese in the TTS settings .

The standard preset is selected by default. Other presets include boosted bass, boosted treble, and others. I will not comment on how each preset sounds because hearing preferences are subjective, and the results can also vary depending on the speakers or earphones being used.

The To top and To end functions can now be used on sliders. These functions are assigned to swiping up then down and down then up with one finger if alternative granularity navigation mode is not being used to move between navigation types. They can also be assigned to user-defined gestures and can be found in the main menu.

When a slider is focused, To top moves it to its minimum value, while To end moves it to its maximum value.

Like other slider adjustment mechanisms, these functions work only on sliders that the screen reader can modify.

During my testing, To end could not move the brightness slider all the way to its maximum value and stopped at 63%. However, it worked correctly on another slider.

Jieshuo now allows users to stop automatic notification reading in three additional situations: when Do not disturb mode is on, when media is playing, and when Jieshuo timers are active.

These options are available in Notification reading settings.

I cannot comment on how reliably these options work because I do not use automatic notification reading on the device I tested with.

After translation functions stopped working because of changes on Google’s end, the new version includes the necessary modifications for translation to work normally again.

The translation issue also affected some AI-related functions, such as image descriptions. These functions use translation to automatically translate results that come in Chinese from vivo AI services into the user’s target language.

I am not sure if this change was introduced earlier. Another user alerted me to it in this version, and I no longer have an older version installed for comparison.

It is now possible to extend the duration of the long press and hold function, which is 59 seconds by default, by tapping the screen once or performing any onscreen gesture. This removes the 59-second limit. To release the button, the user must tap the screen again with one finger. Other gestures do not work to release the button.

I do not know if the button is eventually released after a certain amount of time, but I tested it for 2 minutes and 39 seconds without the button being released.

Note that if the user performs the function again while still in the window, the limitation remains lifted. Only one tap is required to release the button.

Jieshuo no longer automatically moves between home screen pages when automatic page scrolling is disabled. I tested this with Lawnchair, but I do not know whether it works reliably with all launchers.

The changelog also mentions fixes for bugs related to some devices, including Vivo devices and others.

A 20% discount is currently available on all Jieshuo plans. The discount is active until October 5.

en.summary: RealTime AI Cam tells you what your camera is pointed at, out loud, and every part of it runs on your phone. No account, no…
en.body:
Published 30 September 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

RealTime AI Cam tells you what your camera is pointed at, out loud, and every part of it runs on your phone. No account, no ads, nothing to buy. It works in airplane mode, on a subway, or in another country with no data, and nothing the camera sees ever leaves the device.

WHAT IT DOES

LANGUAGES Built for English speakers. It reads English, and translates printed Spanish into English with no internet at all. Other languages download once from Google, then work offline too.

WORKS WITH TALKBACK Every button is labeled, so you can run the whole app without seeing the screen. Nothing is buried behind a gesture you have to discover, and the app tells you what it is doing while it works.

HONEST ABOUT WHAT IT IS The models are small enough to live on your phone, which is exactly why it works with no signal, and it does get things wrong sometimes. It tells you when it is unsure instead of guessing confidently at you.

PRIVATE BY DESIGN

GOOD FOR

Built by one person at Nice Dreamz in Northern California, and the same app is on iPhone. Most of what is in here came from blind and low vision users emailing me and me building it that night. If something does not work with TalkBack, or you want it to do something it does not do yet, email ma ** @ ******* mp.com .

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

The most interesting feature of the app is the Help Me Aim feature, which tries to help blind users with the challenge of taking photos. During my testing, the app was able to take photos that included the subject I wanted to focus on, and the guidance was good overall. However, the subject is not always centred in the photo. For example, when taking a photo of a plant on a table, other furniture in the room was also captured along with the plant. The plant was present but was not at the centre of the photo. I captured photos of a few subjects and confirmed with sighted users that they were present in the photos.

After the photo is captured, a description is generated, and I find the descriptions decent for an offline model. You can also describe a scene using the dedicated What's This feature. After the scene is described, you can ask additional questions either through voice or by typing. You can also save the photo if you find the scene worth keeping.

I found that the object detection often hallucinates objects that aren't present.

Although the app reads the guidance automatically, this is not the case in some other areas. For example, in the text reading feature, which is labeled as English Text to Speech, you have to focus the Detected text item for it to read the recognized text automatically. Also, answers to questions are not read automatically. You have to find them on the screen. My main testing screen reader is Jieshuo, but things could be different with TalkBack.

Overall, the app deserves attention and testing, especially since the developer has shown a clear willingness to improve it, and he is offering it for free without ads. Privacy is also respected because all processing is done offline using the installed on-device model. Speaking of processing, speed might be different across devices. On my Honor 600 Pro, the speed is rather acceptable, both when analysing the view and when answering questions.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

App version: 1.17, Android 16

es.body:
Disponible el número 50 de “Arroba Sonora”, el podcast de tecnología del CTI, que puede descargarse desde el Gestor ONCE de Libros Digitales, el ClubONCE o escucharse a través de las principales plataformas de podcast o desde la Web del CTI.

En este número, con el que “Arroba Sonora” alcanza su edición número 50, se comienza repasando las principales novedades en materia de accesibilidad que incorpora iOS 27 . Se analizarán algunas de las nuevas funciones y mejoras que pueden resultar de especial interés para las personas con ceguera o deficiencia visual grave, así como otros cambios relacionados con la accesibilidad y el uso de los dispositivos de Apple.

A continuación, se presenta TagFit , una aplicación pensada para etiquetar y organizar productos. Durante el episodio se explicará en qué consiste esta herramienta, cuáles son sus principales funcionalidades y de qué manera puede facilitar la identificación, clasificación y organización de distintos productos en el día a día.

También se ofrece una comparativa de las aplicaciones móviles de diferentes cadenas de supermercados e hipermercados para realizar la compra. Se analizarán sus principales características y, especialmente, su grado de accesibilidad y facilidad de uso para las personas con ceguera o deficiencia visual grave, prestando atención a aspectos como la navegación, la identificación de productos, la gestión de la cesta y el proceso de compra.

La edición se completa con la presentación del chatbot de Aena para WhatsApp , una herramienta que permite consultar información relacionada con vuelos y aeropuertos a través de esta popular aplicación de mensajería. Se explicará su funcionamiento y las posibilidades que ofrece para obtener información útil antes y durante un viaje.

El contenido íntegro de “Arroba Sonora” en formato texto puede descargarse desde el Gestor ONCE de Libros Digitales, o consultarse en la sección correspondiente de “Arroba Sonora” dentro de la Web del CTI.

en.title: In-Process 28th September 2026
en.summary: Let’s talk about NVDA 2026.3! NVDA 2026.3 Beta 2 Changes to the Changes Our International Communities Copying last spoken text Talking about NVDA Show Screen Overview NVDA 2026.3 Beta 2 As mentioned last edition, we released NVDA 2026.2 and dived straight into the beta period for NVDA 2026.3. Firstly, do go back and read all… Read More
en.body:
Let’s talk about NVDA 2026.3!

As mentioned last edition, we released NVDA 2026.2 and dived straight into the beta period for NVDA 2026.3 . Firstly, do go back and read all about NVDA 2026.2 if needed, but otherwise, let’s dive into what is coming up in NVDA 2026.3:

This release includes significant performance improvements, improvements to NVDA’s dialogs, and expanded touch screen input.

Several performance improvements have been made to reduce lag and improve responsiveness. NVDA now fetches and caches more information about controls in the background, improving performance in controls such as combo boxes and File Explorer. NVDA no longer causes File Explorer or other applications to crash when NVDA is exited or restarted. NVDA now recovers more quickly when an application stops responding, and will no longer freeze or flood the log with errors from unresponsive applications. In live text regions, such as terminals, NVDA no longer freezes when substantial amounts of text are dumped to the screen.

Context menus and keyboard shortcuts have been added to the Configuration Profiles, Input Gestures, and Speech Dictionaries dialogs, making these dialogs easier to use with the keyboard. It is also now possible to change an existing gesture directly in the Input Gestures dialog. The dialog used to present browsable messages has been modernized and now better supports resizing, maximizing, and minimizing.

Touch screen input has been significantly expanded. Sequential two-flick gestures now combine two flicks in quick succession into a single gesture, greatly increasing the number of bindable touch gestures. Edge gestures are also now supported, allowing gestures that begin within 15 mm of any screen edge to be bound independently from the same gesture performed in the centre of the screen.

A new unassigned command has been added to move the mouse cursor to the centre of the magnified view. Windows OCR can now be used while the Screen Curtain or NVDA’s built-in Magnifier is active.

Liblouis has been updated with new Elfdalian, Sami, Maori, New Zealand Unified English Braille, and Haitian Creole braille tables, a Norwegian table for Spanish text, and additional Swedish 6 and 8 dot variants. eSpeak NG has been updated with added support for Ligurian and Abkhaz.

Updates to translations Fix bug with Magnifier’s “Show screen overview” feature when using relative tracking mode Updated eSpeak In browse mode, alt+upArrow and alt+downArrow now collapse or expand combo boxes in more situations Prevent flashing from shifting magnifier colour filters to reduce seizure risk Update to the Chinese Word Segmentation library cppjieba to fix startup crashes from Chinese paths

If you’ve looked at the changes document for the NVDA 2026.3 betas , you might have noticed a change to the formatting. Or rather, some new formatting. Instead of having a list of features, and then breaking that up into sub-lists of Braille features and Touch Screen features and Browse mode features, we’ve made them headings:

“What’s new in NVDA” is at the top of the document and is a heading level 1 – press shift+1 to jump back to that from anywhere (or control+home since it’s at the top of the document). The version of NVDA, “2026.3”, “2026.2” etc, is a heading level 2. Press 2 to jump to the next older version of NVDA, or shift+2 to jump back to the start of the current version, or next newest version of NVDA. “New features”, “Changes”, “Bug Fixes”, “Changes for Developers”, “Security fixes”, and “Important notes” are all Heading level 3. sub-headings in the section, new features, changes, etc, are heading level 4. In the “New Features” for NVDA 2026.3 for instance, press 4 to jump to “Braille”, “Touch Screen Input”, “Browse Mode”, which are all sections of new features for this version.

If you are used to simply arrowing down through the list and reading each feature, that still works as it did. Or if you press i to jump between list items, that will still work, although you will miss the heading. If you navigate like that and hear “List with x items” and you’re not sure what the list is, press shift+h to jump to the previous heading (at any level) and it will move to the heading just before the list. As something new, we’re interested in what you think – good or bad. It’s the first time we’ve changed the formatting in awhile (though not the first at all, though the last change will not have been as noticeable to all our users).

While we’ve been sprucing things up, we recently gave the “ Connect with the NVDA Community ” page a once over. Firstly, we made sure all the links worked and followed up those with problems. As a result of that, we’ve removed a couple in consultation with their owners (Finnish and Swedish particularly) and added a couple more we had found along the way (Hi to our friends from the Brazilian Portuguese site!)

We also took the opportunity to add headings at H3 for each language, so you can jump or link to the Romanian resources directly now.

We’re always interested in adding new resources to the list. Are you aware of any other groups we’re not aware of? Particularly in languages not yet listed there. Please get in touch if you know of any.

One of the popular features in NVDA 2026.2 was the addition of NVDA+x to repeat the last spoken information. You could press that twice quickly to have the information displayed in a dialog so you could read it with more granular control. If what you want to do is copy the information, while you can do it from that dialog, we’ve added a new command to NVDA 2026.3 to make it even easier. Press NVDA+control+x to copy the last spoken information directly to the clipboard. Thank you to community contributor Cary for his work on this feature!

(A screenshot of the original NVDA+x double press dialog, showing the new feature bullet point for the NVDA+control+x command. Note the dialog has white text on black, because I had the magnifier running with colours inverted when I took the screenshot.)

We love talking about NVDA! I often forget to mention interviews here, but we’ve recently done a couple I thought I’d share:

Access Point Firstly, our “Access Point” collaboration with World Services for the Blind continues with the second in our podcast series, on everything new in NVDA 2026.2.

Tek Talk Next, Training & Support Manager Quentin was on Tek Talk , again covering everything new with NVDA.

And, on a slightly different topic NOT involving us talking – but if YOU love talking about NVDA, accessibility and navigation, Monash University, in Australia, are offering a paid PhD Scholarship in Communication and Navigation for Blind and Low Vision People .

Monash are looking for a linguist or researcher with a related background to investigate how Blind and Low Vision people navigate the world using technology.

The project focuses on video ethnography, multimodal communication, and users’ experiences of navigation technology, with opportunities to collaborate with researchers in assistive technology and AI.

This is open to both Australians and International applicants It’s also part of the Monash Assistive Technology and Society Centre (MATS) and Monash AI Institute so the successful applicant will have lots of opportunity to collaborate with technologists about building better navigational tech going forward.

Do refer to the position description at Monash for all the details.

One of the features of the magnifier we didn’t mention much last time is the Show Entire Screen Overview. Since one of the fixes in the latest NVDA 2026.3 beta is a fix involving this feature, I thought it was worth a mention. So firstly, the fix is that it WILL now work if using relative tracking mode – so if you prefer that magnifier tracking mode, you might want to upgrade before trying it out.

With the magnifier running, press NVDA+shift+L to “Show entire screen”. This temporarily zooms out to show the whole screen (as if the magnifier wasn’t running). After a couple of seconds without the mouse moving, the view zooms back in again.

Because the view smoothly zooms out and then back in again, it makes it easier to tell where the zoomed area is in relation to the whole screen. By waiting for mouse movement to stop, it allows a user to explore the unmagnified view and then smoothly zooms in to where the focus currently is.

If you wish to instantly enable or disable the magnifier, NVDA+shift+w will do this immediately, without zoom out (and then only magnifies again once you press NVDA+shift+w again).

Another difference is that pressing NVDA+shift+L zooms out but leaves any colour filtering enabled. If you wish to quickly zoom out and remove colour filtering, then you may find turning off the magnifier ( NVDA+shift+w ) works better.

And a related tip – if you don’t want magnification BUT do want colour filtering, you can enable the magnifier, enable colour filtering ( NVDA+shift+i ) and then zoom out to 1x ( NVDA+shift+minus ).

That’s all for this week. A little longer than it sometimes is, but there we covered quite a few keystrokes – did you learn any new ones? Surely at least NVDA+control+x ? Do try out the latest 2026.3 beta, and some of those commands. Do please keep giving feedback on the changes and improvements. Also please do share any other international communities we aren’t yet aware of.

Published 26 September 2026 by neirin

PlayNook Interactive Audiobook is an interactive audiobook and story-game app where you listen to narrated stories and make choices that shape what happens next.

Professional voice actors narrate the story while music and sound design build the scene. At key moments, the story pauses and asks you to choose what to do. Choices can be made by tapping or speaking aloud.

The catalog includes fantasy, mystery, horror, romance, and other genres, with original stories, partnerships, community stories, and shorter one-chapter adventures. First chapters are free, with additional content available through in-app purchases.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

The user interface is completely accessible with TalkBack. The main issue reported during story playback is that the state of the play/pause button is announced as each story segment appears and starts playing. On the submitted Samsung device, TalkBack audio is shifted to the phone's internal speakers instead of remaining on the connected headset with the rest of the audio. When the dice appears, an indicator is announced, but TalkBack does not explain that the dice can be rolled or clearly announce that it has appeared.

en.title: LiveComics
en.summary: LiveComics is a comic, manga, and manhwa reader that performs the page as audio rather than simply displaying it. Every speech bubble is voiced in…
en.body:
Published 25 September 2026 by Matt T

LiveComics is a comic, manga, and manhwa reader that performs the page as audio rather than simply displaying it. Every speech bubble is voiced in character, with a separate narrator, while each panel can include its own sound effects and score. The reader advances panel by panel as the scene plays, allowing a whole issue to be followed without seeing the screen.

The app streams a free shelf of classic public-domain issues. Readers can also import their own CBR and CBZ files on the web and read them on the phone.

A free account covers the core service with no card required. A paid storage tier is available through the website, with no in-app purchases.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Tested with TalkBack. A comic is a purely visual medium, and this app performs the whole issue as audio: every line is voiced in character with a separate narrator, the drawn sound effects actually sound, and a score runs under the scene, so a complete story can be followed with the screen off. On navigation, the library, the store, the menus and the reader controls all work without a mouse and report themselves to the screen reader, and cover tiles are real buttons rather than tappable images. Turning a panel announces your position and nothing else, for example "page 3, panel 5 of 40", and that silence is deliberate so the screen reader does not talk over the narration. The panel's own words are available separately, in a hidden region named "Panel text" holding the description, the dialogue line by line and the drawn sound lettering; nothing in it is ever announced on its own, so a braille display can read it without fighting the audio. Dialogs take focus when they open and hand it back when they close, Escape closes them, screen changes are announced politely because the app never reloads the page, and segmented controls report which option is selected. Automated checks are clean, with axe reporting 0 serious or critical issues, though that is a floor rather than a claim about real use. For low vision, the reader crops to a single panel, fills the screen with it and then advances on its own as the scene plays, which is magnification you do not have to drive, with no pinching and no hunting for the next balloon. Known issues and limitations, stated plainly: the "Panel text" region is easy to miss, because it never announces itself and nothing in the reader tells you it is there; Tab is not trapped inside dialogs; the library's medium filter (All, Comics, Manga, Manhwa) does not report which option is currently selected; there is no audio-first onboarding, so signing up and importing a file still assume you can work an ordinary form; the collision between the screen reader and the narration has never been deliberately tested across a range of devices, so we cannot promise the ducking behaves the same everywhere; and NVDA on Windows and iOS VoiceOver have never been run at all, so with the phone app loading the same code as the website, Windows behaviour in particular is unverified.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7, Android 16

en.title: Google Is Rolling Out Guided Vision to Gemini Live: Here’s How to Use It and My Early Impressions
en.summary: Google allows users to turn on the camera feed while in a conversation with Gemini Live, so they can ask about things that are in…
en.body:
Published 23 September 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Google allows users to turn on the camera feed while in a conversation with Gemini Live, so they can ask about things that are in view. Although a blind user can take advantage of this feature, it is not designed specifically to assist blind people. Google is now rolling out Guided vision, a mode that uses the camera in a live conversation to help blind people get an overview of their surroundings, read text, and more. This post covers turning the feature on and using it, as well as my first impressions from testing it.

Note that I haven’t done anything special to access Guided vision on my Honor 600 Pro, but I am running a three-month AI Pro trial that came as an offer with my device, so I don’t know if that affected the feature’s arrival on my device. The feature is not available for my other Accessible Android colleagues yet.

Table of Contents

To enable Guided vision:

A notification appears on the screen with the ability to start a Live session directly. When you use the button to start the Live session, it starts with the camera feed enabled, so you can start talking.

Note that the feature is still not available for everyone, so you should wait if you cannot find the Guided vision toggle in Settings.

According to the Google Accessibility help article , it’s possible to assign Guided vision to an accessibility shortcut, and you can launch it through TalkBack too. However, both are still not available on my device. In fact, I haven’t received any TalkBack update recently.

I haven’t tested to see if launching the camera in a Live conversation when Guided vision is active uses the mode without any user’s intervention, but during my tests, I always asked Gemini to start Guided vision to make sure that it works in that mode. When I tried to prompt the assistant to start the feature, it asked me to point the camera at what I wanted described, but that was one of its hallucinations, as it didn’t open the camera feed or start the Live conversation. Starting a Live conversation is still necessary.

At another time, I asked it to start a Live conversation with Guided vision, but at that instance, it told me that it couldn’t start it automatically and asked me to start Live manually.

Note that turning off Guided vision and then turning it back on from Settings shows the notification to start a Live conversation again, which can be used to start a conversation with the camera turned on.

When I had my first conversation with Live with Guided vision turned on, Gemini reminded me that it cannot detect all hazards or guarantee path clearance and that I should use my mobility aid before almost every response. I kept telling it that I understand the risks and that it shouldn’t repeat those warnings. During the later conversations, I didn’t hear any of the warnings. I am not sure, though, if my early prompting helped, or if you hear those warnings only during the first conversation to alert you of the risks or when Gemini thinks that it should do so for your safety.

During conversations with Guided vision active, I couldn’t find any indication that a special mode is active. All Live-related controls are the same, with no difference. However, the difference is in how Gemini acts. During my short tests, I found that Gemini tried to be detailed in its descriptions because it was aware that Guided vision is active and that the mode is designed to assist blind users.

I was able to ask it questions about the mode, and I got assurance from it that the mode is to assist blind users. It gave me guidance on how to move the camera to show certain objects or scenes better. When I asked it to tell me how to move to reach something, it told me that it needed to know exactly where I was in relation to the camera’s orientation. Using my hand as a reference, it gave me directions with respect to my hand. It also described the positions of items in the room relative to each other, like the position of a fan relative to the sofa.

Additionally, Gemini told me the book that I was holding and tried to assist me in putting the full page in view. When I asked it to read the page, it read a part of the page, though. However, when I asked it if that was the only text on the page, it correctly stated that there were other texts and visual diagrams and offered to describe them for me.

These observations are based on my initial tests, and I haven’t made direct comparisons between using Guided vision with the feature turned on and using the normal Live camera mode with it turned off.

Guided vision changes only how Gemini tries to provide information, as well as making it give more hints to assist a blind user. However, it is still a part of the Live experience. This means that current Live limitations are still present. The most important limitation is the need to prompt it again to tell you about any change, as Live doesn’t have real-time monitoring or continuous picture analysis capabilities.

Another factor worth mentioning is the model used, as Guided vision doesn’t switch Gemini to a more capable AI model than the one that you are using in your Gemini app.

Although image analysis has already advanced and helps in many scenarios, misidentifications are always a part of the formula that shouldn’t be forgotten. For example, a towel hanging on a door was identified more than once as pink, although it wasn’t pink.

Additionally, leveraging the new mode to take pictures still needs work. After Gemini gave me directions to centre my face and I told it to take a photo, it obeyed my order, opened the camera, and took a photo, but that led to the termination of the Live session. That behavior ended the conversation without being able to make sure that the photo was properly captured or without asking any additional questions about what it includes.

Guided vision is an interesting step forward from Google in tailoring Live camera to blind users. Although Google still has the Lookout app , it decided to make Guided vision a part of the Gemini app. Google decided to launch the feature and mention TalkBack as one of the methods to turn it on before releasing a TalkBack update that includes the necessary shortcut. There is even no accessibility service that can be assigned to an accessibility shortcut at the time of writing. However, an interesting thing for users who rely on other screen readers is that using the feature is not tied to having TalkBack running. I am almost sure that Gemini doesn’t check whether a screen reader is running as a requirement to use the feature.

Although it is in its early stages, I am excited to keep Guided vision on, and I am not considering going back to the normal camera mode. This should minimize the need to remind Gemini that I am blind or to try to speak prompts asking it to help me guide my camera toward the subject I am asking about or the text I want it to help me read.

Google doesn’t lack the resources to improve how Guided vision works, with the money and ability to make Gemini Live a trusted assistant, as much as “trusted” can be used with AI services, that understands the needs of blind people and helps them live a more independent life.

Published in Reviews Tutorials

en.title: Accessimind Screen Reader
en.summary: Accessimind Reader is a screen reader application developed to enable visually impaired and partially sighted users to use their Android phones more clearly, quickly, and…
en.body:
Published 19 September 2026 by Sarper Arıkan

Accessimind Reader is a screen reader application developed to enable visually impaired and partially sighted users to use their Android phones more clearly, quickly, and independently.

Accessimind Reader uses the Android AccessibilityService API to provide screen reading functions. AccessibilityService is used to provide audio versions of on-screen content, detect user interface elements, navigate with gestures, provide audio feedback on focused items, and deliver a screen reader experience. This service is necessary for the screen reading feature, which is the core function of the application, to work.

Accessimind Reader does not use AccessibilityService for user tracking, displaying advertisements, remotely recording calls, bypassing Android security mechanisms, or modifying user settings without permission.

The application presents audio feedback, gesture navigation, keyboard shortcuts, clipboard operations, reading preferences, and tools for the focused item in a practical accessibility flow. The context menu provides quick access to frequently used areas such as reading controls, clipboard operations, notification access, focused item operations, and Accessimind settings.

Key Features:

Accessimind Reader is designed for users who need voice output and fast navigation. It focuses on providing predictable controls, understandable labels, and quick access to frequently used screen reader operations.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Accessimind is a screen reader. Users can test it to see how well its features work for them and fit their needs.

Android 16

en.title: Jieshuo Touch Focus And Double Tap Delays
en.summary: Whether you are exploring the screen or trying to find a specific element, there is a delay between touching the screen and focusing on the…
en.body:
Published 16 September 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Whether you are exploring the screen or trying to find a specific element, there is a delay between touching the screen and focusing on the element under your finger. Similar to TalkBack, Jieshuo screen reader allows you to change the value of this delay. It also allows you to set the time in which 2 taps are registered as an accessibility double tap.

In order to change the touch focus delay and double tap delay values, you must first enable handling gestures directly through Jieshuo. To do this, go to Advanced settings > Operation settings and check the Handle gestures in the screen reader checkbox.

The next item in this section is for setting the touch focus delay value. Available values are 150, 200, 250, and 300 milliseconds. To change the time for double tap registration, select Double tap delay and choose any of the available values. The same values as those available for the touch focus delay are provided here.

In the same settings section, you will find an option called One-finger system gesture trigger range, with the following ranges: small, medium, big, and maximum. This setting defines the distance the finger needs to cover when performing one-finger system navigation gestures, such as swiping up from the bottom to go to Home.

Published in Tutorials

en.title: Blind Accessibility Keyboard (BAK)
en.summary: Blind Accessibility Keyboard (BAK) is an Android keyboard for blind and low-vision users. Refined over many years together with blind users, it was rebuilt from…
en.body:
Published 13 September 2026 by Philip Heyse

Blind Accessibility Keyboard (BAK) is an Android keyboard for blind and low-vision users. Refined over many years together with blind users, it was rebuilt from the ground up in summer 2026: modern, faster, and adjustable in great detail.

Two ways to type, both letting you check a key before it is sent:

– Lift to Type: slide your finger over the keys, hear each one, and commit by lifting it – Double Tap to Type: the first tap reads the key, a second tap confirms it

1. Setup and settings:

Setup is guided step by step and confirms out loud when the keyboard is enabled and selected.

The settings screen is made for TalkBack: a switch and its label are read as one element, and sections announced with a “Section:” prefix.

Settings can be saved to a file and restored later. A session log can be exported or e-mailed if you need help.

2. Keyboard layouts:

264 layouts are included. For most languages you can choose between Simple (four rows), Fluent Flow (five rows with numbers), Fluent Flow with Cursor (plus cursor keys), PC (Ctrl, Alt and function keys), PC with Num Pad, and Robo Gear (familiar from standard smartphone keyboards).

Hold the space bar for the Quick Menu to switch layouts. The full list of languages is at the end of this text.

The app itself is translated into 30 languages, including Finnish, Malay and Urdu.

3. What you hear:

– Adjustable speed and pitch, with upper and lower case told apart by pitch – Choice of speech engine, with language, country and voice – Optional NATO alphabet, so “B” and “D” are never confused – Spoken names for punctuation, symbols and emoji – Announcements when the keyboard opens or closes, when you move between letters, numbers, symbols and emoji, and on Shift, Alt or Ctrl changes – Key click sounds in three styles, with adjustable volume – Vibration when typing and on gestures, each switchable separately

4. Voice input:

Start dictation with the microphone key or the Quick Menu, and choose between:

– Your device’s own dictation – A model running on your device: no account needed, works offline, though less accurate than the online options – Popular AI services, using your own API key, stored encrypted on your device only

5. Typing support:

– Auto-correct for many of the supported languages. One Backspace restores the original word. Never runs in password fields. – Text shortcuts: “brt” becomes “Best regards, Tom”. One Backspace undoes it. – Clipboard history above the keys. Tap an entry to insert it. – Your own keys for text you often need, such as your e-mail address – Optional capital letter at the start of a sentence – Adjustable delay and repeat speed when holding Delete or Backspace

6. Subscription:

BAK is funded by a small subscription. It costs less than the equivalent of one US dollar per month, and follows the local price level, so in many countries it is lower. It pays for ongoing work: fixing bugs, keeping up with new Android versions, and adding features. Before subscribing, you can try the keyboard in the test field on the app’s home screen. A subscription is needed to use it in other apps.

7. Help and contact: – https://bright-side.de/bak/ – ba * @ ********* de.de

The Help section in the app has the documentation, the mailing list, and a way to e-mail the developer.

8. Layouts for your language:

Arabic (also with French), Belarusian, Bengali, Bulgarian (Cyrillic, Latin, Phonetic), Canadian (also French, Multilingual), Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English (UK, USA), French (France, Switzerland), German (Germany, Switzerland), Greek, Gujarati, Hebrew, Hindi (also InScript), Hungarian, Indonesian, Italian (Italy, Switzerland), Kannada, Marathi, Norwegian, Persian, Polish (also programmer), Portuguese (also Brazilian ABNT), Punjabi, Romanian, Russian, Serbian, Spanish (Spain, Latin America), Swedish, Tamil, Telugu, Turkish (F and Q), Ukrainian, Vietnamese.
